# Feature engineering {#sec-features}

```{python}
exec(open("_common.py").read())
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from canes_cfb.features import FEATURE_SETS, FEATURE_SETS_V2, SLATE, cumulative_sets, ridge_ratings, team_games
from canes_cfb.validation import walk_forward

g = games()
feat = features()
```

## The as-of rule

A feature for a game may only use games **played before it**. Using the game's own
result, or anything later, is *leakage*: the backtest looks great and the model fails
in real life.

In practice, features are computed per **slate** (season, season type, week) from
earlier slates only. A Saturday game never sees Thursday's result from the same week,
which also matches what's known when lines are bet midweek. The rule is enforced by a
test (`tests/test_features.py`): building the features with every future result
**hidden** must produce exactly the same values as building them with full data. Both
the score-based and the CFBD-based features pass it.

Only FBS-vs-FBS games feed ratings and form; FCS blowouts would distort them.

## Opponent-adjusted ratings

Scoring 40 against a bad defense isn't the same as scoring 40 against a good one. The
core feature, following @cfbd_ridge, solves for every offense and defense at once.
Before each slate $s$, fit on prior team-games $i$:

$$
\text{points}_i \;=\; \mu \;+\; o_{\text{team}(i)} \;-\; d_{\text{opp}(i)} \;+\; h \cdot \text{hfa}_i \;+\; \varepsilon_i,
\qquad \text{hfa}_i \in \{+1, 0, -1\},
$$

where $o$ is offensive strength, $d$ defensive strength (higher is better), and $h$ the
home edge. Coefficients are estimated with **ridge regression** and **recency
weights**:

$$
\min_{\mu, o, d, h} \; \sum_i w_i \big(\text{points}_i - \hat{\text{points}}_i\big)^2
\;+\; \alpha \big(\lVert o \rVert^2 + \lVert d \rVert^2 + h^2\big),
\qquad w_i = 2^{-\text{age}_i / \tau},
$$

with $\text{age}_i$ in days and half-life $\tau$. The training window is 600 days, so in
September last season acts as the prior, and current form takes over as games
accumulate. Ridge shrinks teams with little data toward average. The model's own
prediction for a matchup is

$$
\text{exp\_points} = \mu + o_{\text{team}} - d_{\text{opp}} + h \cdot \text{hfa}.
$$

### Tuning α and τ

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ridge-grid
#| tbl-cap: "MAE of exp_points alone (team points, 2017–2023) for each shrinkage α and recency half-life τ (days)."
tg = team_games(g)
ev = tg[tg.completed & tg.fbs_game & tg.season.between(2017, 2023)]
grid = []
for alpha in (0.3, 1, 3, 8):
    for hl in (60, 120, 240):
        rr = ridge_ratings(tg, alpha=alpha, half_life_days=hl)
        opp = rr[[*SLATE, "team_id", "def"]].rename(columns={"team_id": "opp_id", "def": "opp_def"})
        m = ev.merge(rr, on=[*SLATE, "team_id"]).merge(opp, on=[*SLATE, "opp_id"])
        pred = m.intercept + m.off - m.opp_def + m.hfa_pts * m.hfa
        grid.append({"alpha": alpha, "half-life": hl, "MAE": (m.points - pred).abs().mean()})
grid = pd.DataFrame(grid).pivot(index="alpha", columns="half-life", values="MAE").round(3)
grid
```

$\alpha = 1$, $\tau = 120$ days wins. Heavy shrinkage ($\alpha = 8$) squeezes every team
toward average; a short memory ($\tau = 60$) forgets last season too fast for September.
An early version used $\alpha = 25$ and compressed every rating to about ±1 point; that
bug and its fix are in @sec-decisions.

The same machinery is reused for **any per-game offensive stat** (plays, EPA per play,
success rate, explosiveness, pass and rush EPA). The target is standardized before
fitting, so $\alpha$ means the same shrinkage for every stat; coefficients are returned
in the stat's own units.

## Elo with a nonlinear margin of victory

A second rating, FiveThirtyEight-style [@fte_elo]. After each game,

$$
R' = R + K \cdot M \cdot (S - E), \qquad
E = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{-\Delta/400}}, \qquad
M = \ln(|\text{MOV}| + 1) \cdot \frac{2.2}{0.001\,\Delta_w + 2.2},
$$

with $K = 25$, home edge 55 Elo points, and one-third regression to 1500 each
offseason. The logarithm gives diminishing credit for blowouts (a 40-point win is worth
little more than a 30-point win). The second factor corrects autocorrelation: favorites
win by more, which would otherwise inflate their rating [@morse_elo].

## Feature families

```{python}
#| label: tbl-families
#| tbl-cap: "Feature families and their sizes."
fams = {**FEATURE_SETS, **FEATURE_SETS_V2}
desc = {
    "raw_form": "points for/against, season-to-date and last 3, relative to league average",
    "ratings": "ridge offense/defense for team and opponent, exp_points",
    "elo": "Elo, opponent Elo, difference",
    "matchup": "explicit interactions: off × opp_def, expected margin, |margin|, margin², residual form, volatility",
    "context": "neutral site, conference game, rest days and difference, bowl, early season, indoor, week",
    "efficiency": "ridge-adjusted tempo, EPA/play, success rate, explosiveness, pass/rush EPA",
    "pace_x_efficiency": "expected plays × expected EPA/play, game pace, pass-vs-rush edge",
    "priors": "talent composite and returning production, team and opponent",
    "preseason": "transfer portal, recruiting classes, new head coach, preseason AP poll (adopted later; @sec-improvements)",
}
pd.DataFrame({"features": {k: len(v) for k, v in fams.items()}, "what": desc})
```

## Which families earn their place?

Walk-forward cross-validation (train on every season before, validate on each of
2019–2023; @sec-modeling). Families are added one at a time. Ridge is linear;
"LightGBM on residual" learns `points − exp_points`, so the ratings carry the signal and
the trees correct what they miss.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ablation
#| tbl-cap: "Cross-validated MAE (points per team, 2019–2023) as feature families are added."
data = feat[feat.completed & feat.season.between(2016, 2023) & ~feat.shortened & feat.market_points.notna()].reset_index(drop=True)
y, ep = data.points.to_numpy(), data.exp_points.to_numpy()

def cv(make, cols, residual):
    errs = []
    for _, tr, va in walk_forward(data):
        t = y - ep if residual else y
        pred = make().fit(data.loc[tr, cols], t[tr]).predict(data.loc[va, cols])
        errs.append(np.abs(y[va] - pred - (ep[va] if residual else 0)).mean())
    return np.mean(errs)

ridge = lambda: make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True), StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=10.0))
resid = lambda: lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.02, num_leaves=7, min_child_samples=200,
                                  subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=0.8, verbose=-1)
rows = []
for name, cols in cumulative_sets().items():
    rows.append({"features": name, "Ridge": cv(ridge, cols, False), "LightGBM on residual": cv(resid, cols, True)})
abl = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("features")
va = data.season >= 2019
ref = pd.DataFrame({"Ridge": [np.abs(y - data.league_avg)[va].mean(), np.abs(y - ep)[va].mean(), np.abs(y - data.market_points)[va].mean()]},
                   index=["baseline: league average", "ratings formula alone", "market: closing line"])
pd.concat([ref, abl]).map(lambda v: "—" if pd.isna(v) else f"{v:.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-ablation
#| fig-cap: "Error as families are added (LightGBM on residual), against the league-average baseline and the closing line."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3))
xs = range(len(abl))
ax.plot(xs, abl["LightGBM on residual"], color=BLUE, marker="o", markersize=5, label="model")
ax.axhline(ref.loc["market: closing line", "Ridge"], color=ORANGE, lw=1.5, ls="--")
ax.text(len(abl) - 1, ref.loc["market: closing line", "Ridge"] + 0.02, "closing line", ha="right", color=INK_2, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xticks(list(xs)); ax.set_xticklabels(abl.index, rotation=30, ha="right", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("MAE (points per team)"); bar_ends(ax); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Note: the "LightGBM on residual" column always starts from the ratings' prediction
(it learns `points − exp_points`), so even its `raw_form` row already contains the
ratings. That's why it starts near 9.44, not near 10.

The reading:

- **Opponent adjustment is the big win.** The league average misses by ~11.1; the ratings
  alone by ~9.44. Raw form (unadjusted points) only reaches ~10.0.
- Elo, explicit matchup terms and context add almost nothing on top of the ratings.
- **CFBD efficiency** helps a bit (~9.38), and **talent and returning production** help
  most among the new families (~9.30), mainly by fixing early weeks.
- The explicit pace × efficiency product adds nothing: trees already combine plays and
  efficiency on their own.
- The **closing line** is still better (~8.91). The gap is information, not model
  complexity, which is what @sec-nonlinearity investigates.
